header.title: Bartholomäus (M1) (München, Staatsbibl., Cgm 92, Bl. 1-20): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:rem:anonymous:m302:norm, from the Referenzkorpus Mittelhochdeutsch, ReM 2.1 (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.9v.b.4: 9v.b.8: 'pibinella' (Latin pimpinella) may be burnet or burnet-saxifrage.
notes.7v.a.10: 7v.a.11: 'stich', literally 'a stitch', i.e. not the least thing.
notes.13v.a.15: Line 13v.a.17 is absent from the edition as given; no text seems lost.
notes.8v.a.23: 8v.b.4: 'einhalp', 'on one side' or 'in one direction'. 8v.b.7-8: the charm is only partly intelligible: N. stands for the patient's name; caro 'flesh', confirma 'make firm'; 'carice' is unexplained; 'Ysmaheli te' may be 'Ishmael ... you', or a single word 'Ishmaelite' split across the line.
notes.12v.a.1: 12v.a.7-8: the letters are given as written. 12v.a.10-14: the test seems to lack a step; it does not say how the worms give the answer. 12v.b.6-7: 'büechînen bluot' is read as 'beech blossom' ('den bluot' in the next line is masculine); if 'bluot' is 'blood', the old stone remedy of dried goat's blood may be meant.
notes.16r.b.27: 16r.b.27: 'himelbrant' taken as mullein. 16v.a.18-19: 'durch daz diu erzenîe îndorre' is read as 'so that the medicine [the parts] may dry'.
notes.13r.b.25: 13r.b.25-26: 'and' is written twice across the line break. 13v.a.2-3: 'dierne', 'girl, maiden', here in the sense 'virgin'.

nodes.text: for a year, so that he never
saw a jot, he will come to see.
If worms hollow out someone's teeth
and eat away the gums, take
henbane oil, and knead it with
wax, and make a candle,
and stand it in a bowl in which there
is a little water. When the
candle is burning, hold the teeth
over it; then the worms fall
all into the water. ¶ If anyone's
kidneys swell, let him take
strap in front of the swelling; then
the person will be well in three days.
When you are told
that a person is bleeding heavily, then
send your messenger for water,
and command the messenger that he
say nothing at all on the way. When the
water has been brought to you, strain it
on one side through your shirt into a
second vessel, and then say these
words: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
N., flesh, *carice*, make firm, *Ysmaheli*
*te*. Do that three times, and give the
messenger [it] to drink, if he is not there
who is bleeding. Truly, it stops just as
quickly. When you feel pain in any
place, in a limb, or otherwise from
any swelling, you need
for half a day. This ointment you can
keep as long as you like.
If you want to test whether the wounded man
will die or recover, take
*pibinella* and grind it up in water,
and give him the herb, so, in the
water, to drink. If he is to recover,
he digests the herb; if he is to die,
you will find the herb in the wound.
When a person's hands or
feet crack, take rue
with rose oil, so that none of the sickness
remains. If it happens that
the fever arises from the sickness, so that
you cannot sleep, take
mallow and violets and poppy,
and boil the three in
water, and set the legs in it
up to the knees. When you have then
soaked them well, anoint the feet
underneath, on the soles, with *populeon* [poplar ointment]
or with rose oil. ¶ When the ears
buzz after the fever, boil eggs
in water so that they become hard, and
fasting, early in the morning,
for seven days; then you will be well.
If you want to bring it about that
your enemies must avoid you,
then write on a [piece of] lead or on
a tin tablet his name
and these letters: h.
h. S. it. l. V. P., and carry
the writing under your foot.
If you want to find out which
woman likes to have a man, then
take turnips and crush them in a
linen cloth; after a while
you will find worms in it.
Whoever wants to bring it about that
the dogs do not bark at him,
let him carry in his hand a weasel's
tail, and hare's hair in the other,
or let him have a dog's
heart about him, and carry a
dog's tongue under his big
toe. If you want to catch birds
with your hand: a plant is called
*Cicuta*, which means hemlock.
Take this same plant, and wine lees,
and when you get the juice
out of the plant, mix the
lees with the juice, and steep
wheat in it. Whatever bird
eats of it cannot
fly. If you want to break up the stone
quickly, take beech
blossom and dry it in the sun
and boil the root with it, and
and anoint the head; then
the hair grows. Take smallage and burn
it and hold it under the nose of a woman
who says she is a maiden.
If she is not a maiden, she wets
herself. When you
have strangury, take
mallow and garlic and
gets no relief from this powder
very certainly has the stone.
There is a herb called *Verbena* [vervain], which
is useful for many things
and good. Of this same herb
virtues as there are
twigs growing on it.
If you want to help a person
with the falling sickness [epilepsy], take
a new strap of deerskin. When
the sickness seizes him, bind it
around his neck while he is suffering, and
say: In the name of the Father
and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
I bind here the sickness
of this person in this knot.
And take the strap and tie
a knot in it,
and bind the strap
around his neck. And
the person shall then abstain
from wine until he
comes to where a dead man
is buried. There one shall untie, for the sick man,
the strap from his neck
and shall bury the strap
with the dead man,
and shall put it under the dead man's
shoulder. And let him say,
who unties the strap: In the name
of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit I bury
with this strap the sickness
of this person, on the condition
that to this person
this sickness will never again do harm
until this body
rises on the Last Day.
With these words one shall
bury the strap under the dead man's
shoulder. If he is not there
who first bound the strap,
then let another untie it
and bury it as that one
should have done, and as is written
here; then the sickness will trouble him
no more. ¶ When the person cannot keep
food down and has to vomit,
help him thus: take betony
let him boil mullein, root and all,
and bind it on his leg;
he will be relieved of it. Jerome,
the holy man, found in the Chaldean
books, concerning many a
remedy that is in many a bird.
Among these same birds he found,
concerning the vulture, such great
medicine that he declared: as many
remedies were in the vulture as
it has members. He says
thus: whoever wants the vulture for medicine
must take care to kill it
without iron, before it becomes aware of it,
for if it understands that it cannot
survive, it swallows its
brain. So when the vulture is
caught, one should then take it entirely
apart, limb by limb, so that the medicine
does not dry out. There is no medicine at all,
